title: Banned Words

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (Aho-Corasick automaton), cf. CSES String Matching and Word Combinations

statement:
A moderation tool scans a message `text` for `k` banned words. For every banned word, report how many times it occurs in the message. Occurrences may **overlap**, and the same word may appear in the list more than once (each copy then gets the same answer).

**Input.** First line: `text`. Second line: `k`. Then `k` lines, one banned word each.

**Output.** `k` lines: the number of occurrences of each word, in the order given.
constraints: Lowercase letters only; no word is empty
1 ≤ |text| ≤ 20000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 1000, total length of the words ≤ 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 10^6)

hints: Running KMP once per word costs O(|text|) per word, so O(k · |text|) overall. Look for a single pass over the text that handles every word at once.

Put all words in a trie. While reading the text keep the trie node for the longest suffix of the text read so far that is a prefix of some word. If the next letter has no edge, fall back to the node for the next-longest such suffix: the **failure link**, computed by BFS exactly like the prefix function.

Fill in the missing transitions using the failure links so each text letter moves the automaton in O(1). Count how many times each node is visited, then add each node's count to its failure link's count in reverse BFS order: a visit to a node is also an occurrence of every word that is a suffix of it.
editorial: Build a **trie** of all words and turn it into the **Aho-Corasick automaton**. Each node represents a prefix of some word; its *failure link* points to the node for the longest proper suffix of that prefix that is also a trie prefix. A BFS from the root computes them: for a child `u = go[v][c]`, `fail[u] = go[fail[v]][c]`, and a missing transition `go[v][c]` is filled with `go[fail[v]][c]`, so the structure becomes a full automaton where each text character costs one array lookup. Scan the text, incrementing `cnt[v]` for the node `v` reached after each character. An occurrence of a word ends at every position where the automaton is in the node of that word **or in any node that has the word as a suffix**, so propagate counts up the failure tree: process nodes in reverse BFS order doing `cnt[fail[v]] += cnt[v]`. The answer for a word is `cnt` at its end node; duplicate words simply share a node. Total time is `O(total word length · 26 + |text|)`, and memory is `O(total word length · 26)`.

solutions.python:
import sys
from collections import deque
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
text = data[0]
k = int(data[1])
pats = data[2:2 + k]
nxt = [[-1] * 26]                      # trie, later turned into a full automaton
ends = []
for p in pats:
    v = 0
    for ch in p:
        c = ord(ch) - 97
        if nxt[v][c] < 0:
            nxt.append([-1] * 26)
            nxt[v][c] = len(nxt) - 1
        v = nxt[v][c]
    ends.append(v)                      # duplicate patterns share one node
size = len(nxt)
fail = [0] * size
order = []
q = deque()
for c in range(26):
    u = nxt[0][c]
    if u < 0:
        nxt[0][c] = 0
    else:
        q.append(u)
while q:
    v = q.popleft()
    order.append(v)
    for c in range(26):
        u = nxt[v][c]
        if u < 0:
            nxt[v][c] = nxt[fail[v]][c]          # follow the failure link for missing transitions
        else:
            fail[u] = nxt[fail[v]][c]
            q.append(u)
cnt = [0] * size
v = 0
for ch in text:
    v = nxt[v][ord(ch) - 97]
    cnt[v] += 1                          # the text is at node v right now
for v in reversed(order):                # every match at v is also a match of its failure suffix
    cnt[fail[v]] += cnt[v]
print("\n".join(str(cnt[e]) for e in ends))
